title: Relational Algebra & Calculus
summary: The math behind SQL. Learn the operators that define what every query can do — and why algebra says how while calculus says what.

blocks.markdown:
**Relational algebra** is the formal theory behind SQL — a set of operations on tables that produce new tables.

- Every SQL query maps to algebra; the database engine uses it to plan execution.
- **Algebra** is *procedural* — you describe the steps (select, then join, then project).
- **Relational calculus** is *declarative* — you describe only the result, not the steps.
- Knowing both helps you read query plans and ace DB interviews. See [relational-model-keys](relational-model-keys).

blocks.subTitle: Selection & Projection
blocks.markdown:
The two most-used unary operators (one input table).

- **σ (sigma) — Selection:** filters *rows* by a condition. σ_{age>30}(Emp) keeps only employees over 30.
- **π (pi) — Projection:** keeps chosen *columns*. π_{name,dept}(Emp) drops all other columns.

Combined: π_{name}(σ_{dept='HR'}(Emp)) — names of HR employees.

blocks.subTitle: Set operators
blocks.markdown:
Binary operators borrowed from set theory. Both relations must be **union-compatible** (same number of columns, matching types).

- **∪ Union:** all rows from both tables, duplicates removed.
- **− Set difference:** rows in the first table but not the second.
- **∩ Intersection:** rows that appear in both.

Example: Students ∪ Alumni = everyone who was ever enrolled.

blocks.subTitle: Cartesian product & Rename
blocks.markdown:
- **× Cartesian product:** every row of A paired with every row of B. If A has m rows and B has n, result has m×n rows. Rarely used alone — the base of joins.
- **ρ (rho) — Rename:** gives a table or column a new name. Needed when joining a table to itself to avoid ambiguity.

ρ_{E2}(Emp) creates alias E2 for Emp.

blocks.subTitle: Theta, Equi & Natural join
blocks.markdown:
A join = cartesian product filtered by a condition.

- **Theta join (⋈_θ):** any comparison condition (A.salary > B.budget).
- **Equi join:** theta join where condition is equality (A.deptId = B.id). Most common.
- **Natural join (⋈):** auto-equi-joins on *all* matching column names, then drops duplicate columns.

Natural join is convenient but fragile — adding a same-named column can silently break queries.

blocks.subTitle: Outer joins
blocks.markdown:
Outer joins keep rows that have no match, filling missing columns with **NULL**.

| Variant | Keeps non-matching rows from |
|---|---|
| Left outer ⟕ | Left table |
| Right outer ⟖ | Right table |
| Full outer ⟗ | Both tables |

Left join: all employees including those with no department. See [sql-basics-joins](sql-basics-joins).

blocks.subTitle: Division
blocks.markdown:
**Division (÷):** finds rows in A that are paired with *every* row in B.

- A(student, course) ÷ B(course) → students enrolled in **all** courses in B.
- Think: "which students took all required courses?"
- SQL has no direct DIVISION keyword; it's expressed with NOT EXISTS or double negation.

Division is rare in practice but a favourite exam question.

blocks.subTitle: Aggregation
blocks.markdown:
Pure relational algebra has no aggregation; extended algebra adds the **G (gamma) operator**.

- Notation: _{groupCols} **G** _{aggFuncs}(R). E.g., dept **G** count(empId), avg(salary)(Emp).
- Aggregation functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX.
- Maps directly to SQL's GROUP BY ... HAVING.

Extended algebra also adds **outer union** for non-union-compatible tables.

blocks.subTitle: Tuple Relational Calculus (TRC)
blocks.markdown:
**TRC** describes the result using tuple variables and logical conditions — no steps, just the shape of the answer.

- Form: `{ t | P(t) }` — all tuples t satisfying predicate P.
- Example: `{ t | t ∈ Emp ∧ t.dept = 'HR' }` — same as σ_{dept='HR'}(Emp).
- Uses ∃ (exists) and ∀ (for all) quantifiers.
- **Safe expression:** one whose result is always finite (must be bounded by the actual database).

blocks.subTitle: Domain Relational Calculus (DRC)
blocks.markdown:
**DRC** uses domain variables (one per column) instead of whole tuple variables.

- Form: `{ <x1,x2,...> | P(x1,x2,...) }` — listing column values satisfying P.
- Example: `{ <n,d> | <n,d,_> ∈ Emp ∧ d = 'HR' }` — names and depts of HR staff.
- QBE (Query By Example), an early visual query language, was based on DRC.
- Both TRC and DRC are equivalent in power to relational algebra (Codd's theorem).

The central contrast of this topic.

| | Relational Algebra | Relational Calculus |
|---|---|---|
| Style | Procedural (how) | Declarative (what) |
| Specifies | Step-by-step ops | Result description |
| SQL maps to | Query plan steps | Query syntax |

SQL is declarative like calculus; the optimizer translates it to algebra internally. Both are equally powerful — a query expressible in one can be expressed in the other.

Common mistakes:

- **Natural join surprise:** columns are matched by name, not meaning. A column named `id` in both tables joins on that, even if it's unrelated.
- **Projection loses duplicates:** π removes duplicate rows by definition — algebra works on sets, not bags (unlike SQL's default).
- **Division ≠ SQL DIVIDE:** SQL has no direct operator; getting it wrong in exams is common.
- **Unsafe TRC:** a formula with ¬∃ can produce infinite results if not bounded by a relation.

blocks.subTitle: Algebra vs calculus
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between relational algebra and relational calculus?**

**Algebra** is procedural — you spell out the operators step by step (select, join, project). **Calculus** is declarative — you describe what the result looks like using predicates, not how to compute it. SQL is closer to calculus in style; the query optimizer converts it to algebra internally. Both have identical expressive power (Codd's theorem).

blocks.subTitle: Natural join vs equi join
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between a natural join and an equi join?**

An **equi join** is a theta join whose condition is equality — you explicitly name the columns. A **natural join** automatically joins on all columns with the same name and removes the duplicate column. Natural join is shorter to write but fragile: a new column with a matching name in either table silently changes the join semantics.

blocks.subTitle: What division computes
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What does the division operator compute and when is it used?**

Division A ÷ B returns rows in A that are associated with *every* row in B. Classic use: "find students enrolled in all required courses." SQL doesn't have a DIVIDE keyword — you express it with double NOT EXISTS. It's rare in production but appears often in theory exams.

blocks.subTitle: Why algebra matters for SQL
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why should a developer know relational algebra if they just write SQL?**

The query optimizer rewrites your SQL into an algebra expression tree and picks the cheapest equivalent form (e.g., push σ before a join to reduce rows early). Reading EXPLAIN output is much easier when you know what selection, projection, and join steps look like. It also makes you write queries the optimizer can push down efficiently.
